extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, newsroom leaders, and readers interested in media industry practices and ethics
extracted.subtask_description: A daily Poynter newsletter summarizing recent media stories, industry developments, and commentary about journalistic practice, ethics, and business strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish detailed corrections and prioritize truth over pride
rubrics_metrics.description: When errors are discovered, publish a comprehensive correction that lists and explains each error and update the story as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Washington Post published a 579-word correction covering 15 items and updated the story based on re-reporting by Post staff. The author applauds putting truth over pride even when the correction invites condemnation and ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerate each error and re-report as necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrections should be specific, covering every inaccuracy or needed clarification rather than vague statements that something was 'fixed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Post's approach—detailed correction of each error and updating the story based on re-reporting—serves as a model for transparency and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous vetting of freelancers and stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms must properly vet freelance contributors and ensure sufficient fact-checking and editorial oversight before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece questions 'how in the world did this story get published?' and urges that publications—even high-profile ones—should investigate vetting practices to prevent a high volume of mistakes in a single story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and internal investigation after major errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and leadership should perform internal reviews and 'soul searching' when widespread errors occur to restore reader confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mistakes 'erode reader confidence' and do real damage; the newsroom should do serious investigating into editorial failures when many errors appear in a single piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headlines must accurately reflect content and be corrected promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines that mislead should be acknowledged and amended quickly to match the underlying reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New York Times changed an admitted 'bad headline' for later editions; quick correction is preferable to leaving misleading headlines unaddressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disproportionate consumer responses to isolated mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate mistakes proportionally; a single headline or isolated error should not prompt wholesale abandonment of a news organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that cancelling subscriptions over one headline is 'absurd' given the broader, consistent journalism produced by large newsrooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in editorial quality and maintain newsroom staffing
rubrics_metrics.description: Sustained investment in editorial resources and staffing is a core strategy for building and retaining readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New York Times' strategy to invest in editorial quality and reach a record staffing level (1,750 journalists) is cited as central to its digital subscription growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance customer acquisition spending with retention to manage costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Marketing and promotional spending to attract subscribers must be balanced against churn and overall profitability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Times missed profit expectations partly because of heavy expense promoting new subscriptions and churn as trial offers expire; this is a reminder to weigh promotional tactics against retention outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose documentary topics that are unresolved and layered
rubrics_metrics.description: Documentary journalism should explore stories that remain unresolved and have layers of complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ESPN's new series 'Backstory' aims to 'explore stories that are unresolved and have layers to them,' using examples like Serena Williams' U.S. Open final and the Black Sox scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: When cutting print frequency, ensure continuity of coverage and digital access
rubrics_metrics.description: If a paper reduces print days, it must preserve news coverage quality and make content available digitally around the clock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McClatchy plans expanded Friday and Sunday sections, commits to putting news online 24 hours a day (including Saturdays), and frames the change as a push toward promoting the digital product—readers should expect no reduction in coverage even as print frequency falls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor hiring commitments and treat recruits ethically
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should avoid rescinding accepted job offers whenever possible and recognize the human impact of such decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rescinding of a job offer to a young sportswriter after a hiring freeze is characterized as 'disgraceful'; the author suggests employers should find ways to honor offers or handle cutbacks more responsibly.
